title: Restaurant busy season checklist for owners
seoTitle: Restaurant busy season checklist for owners | ROAL
description: Use this restaurant busy season checklist to prep phones, staff, hours, menus, and call forwarding before the rush hits.
question: What should I put on a restaurant busy season checklist before the rush starts?
answer: A good restaurant busy season checklist covers phone coverage, hours, menu updates, staff roles, and pickup order flow before the rush starts. It should also tell callers what to expect, set up call forwarding for busy periods, and give staff a simple plan for high-volume shifts.
summary: A practical checklist to prepare your phones, menu, staff, and call flow before busy season hits.
intro:
Busy season for a restaurant starts before the line forms. The best restaurant busy season checklist covers phones, menu updates, hours, staffing, and pickup order flow so service stays steady when calls spike.

If you run a pizza shop, deli, takeout spot, or family restaurant, the goal is simple: answer faster, take cleaner orders, and keep the kitchen from getting buried. Tools like ROAL can help with phone coverage, but the real win comes from a short, practical plan your team can follow.

sections.h2: What should I check on the phone before the rush starts?
sections.body:
Start with the phone, because that is where a lot of busy-season pain shows up first. Make sure callers hear the right hours, the right address, and the right pickup info. If your lunch rush or dinner rush usually swamps the line, decide now whether calls will ring through normally, forward when busy, or forward only when unanswered.

A simple phone checklist:
- Test the main number from a cell phone.
- Confirm the greeting says your current hours.
- Confirm the address and parking directions are right.
- Check that voicemail is not sitting there as the backup plan.
- Decide who handles allergy questions, catering questions, and manager requests.

A useful script line for staff is: “Thanks for calling. We’re in the dinner rush, so I may need a moment while I take your order.” That keeps the caller calm and buys you time.

If you use [call forwarding codes by carrier](/tools/call-forwarding-codes), confirm the right code with your phone company and test it with a real call. Codes vary by carrier and plan, and many restaurants use forwarding only during the busiest hours.

sections.h2: How do I keep menu changes from slowing down orders?
sections.body:
Busy season exposes every menu problem fast. If an item is sold out, if a price changed, or if a combo is no longer available, the phone team needs to know right away. The fastest fix is to update the menu before the rush, then keep one person responsible for same-day changes.

Use this menu prep checklist:
1. Remove sold-out items from the phone script and menu board.
2. Confirm prices for your top sellers.
3. Check sizes, modifiers, and add-ons for your most-ordered items.
4. Write out any common substitutions, like “no onions” or “extra cheese.”
5. Make sure allergy-sensitive questions go to staff, not to guesswork.

A practical example: say your best-selling pie is $28, your extra topping is $2, and your delivery order usually adds one topping. The caller’s total is easy to quote if the menu is current. If your pricing changes for busy season, plug in your own numbers before the rush and make sure the whole team sees the same version.

ROAL reads menu, prices, hours, and address from public pages or an uploaded menu, then lets the owner edit the menu later from the dashboard. That matters when you need a quick change and do not want the phones to get tied up with “What does that come with?” all night.

sections.h2: How many people do I need on the floor and in the kitchen?
sections.body:
Busy season staffing is not only about having enough people. It is about putting the right people in the right spots. A strong schedule separates order taking, expo, prep, packing, and pickup handoff so no one gets pulled in three directions.

Use a simple role plan:
- One person watches the register and pickup shelf.
- One person handles make-line or kitchen tickets.
- One person answers the phone during the rush, or checks the phone host inbox between rushes.
- One backup person can step in if a line gets long.

Worked example: if your dinner rush usually brings 30 phone orders in two hours, that is 15 orders per hour. If each order takes a few minutes to take correctly, you can see why one person on the phone may get buried. Plug in your own order count and your own average ticket time, then decide whether you need extra coverage or a phone host doing the first pass.

A good staff instruction is: “Take the order, repeat it once, and send the caller to the next step.” Keep the wording short. Busy season is not the time for long explanations at the counter.

sections.h2: How should I handle pickup orders when calls stack up?
sections.body:
Pickup is where the busy-season checklist becomes real. If the phone is busy, the order still has to land clearly in the kitchen and the customer still needs a ready time they trust. Clean order flow matters more than a fancy system.

For pickup orders, check these items:
- Caller name and phone number.
- Items, sizes, modifiers, and notes.
- Ready time quoted back clearly.
- Any allergy note handed to staff with a summary.
- Sold-out items blocked before the caller hears them.

A helpful phone line is: “I have your order for one large pepperoni, one chicken parm sub, and a side salad. It’ll be ready in about 20 minutes. May I have your name and best callback number?” That script keeps the order tight and confirms the handoff.

ROAL can take pickup and delivery orders from the live menu, collect the caller’s name and phone, quote a ready time, and send a clean ticket to the kitchen screen. It also speaks the caller’s language and hands tricky calls like complaints, catering, allergies, and manager requests to staff with a summary. It does not take card numbers over the phone, so payment still happens the way your restaurant already handles it.

sections.h2: What should I tell customers before they even call?
sections.body:
Busy season gets easier when callers know what to expect. Put the most common answers where people can hear them quickly: hours, holiday changes, parking, pickup rules, and any service limits. If the answer is always the same, the phone should not waste time on it.

Use this short checklist for caller info:
- Current hours.
- Full address and parking notes.
- Pickup and delivery rules.
- The most common menu questions.
- Any holiday or special schedule changes.

Example phone wording: “We’re open until 9 tonight, parking is behind the building, and pickup orders are ready at the side door.” That one sentence can prevent three follow-up calls.

If your phone host handles questions, keep the answers simple and updated. ROAL answers questions about hours, address, parking, and the menu from the live information you give it. Questions it cannot answer land in your inbox, and once you answer them, the host knows it from then on. That is useful when you keep hearing the same questions every Friday or during a holiday week. For more setup ideas, see [setting up a restaurant phone system](/blog/restaurant-phone-system-setup).

sections.h2: How do I set up call forwarding without making a mess?
sections.body:
Call forwarding can help during the rush, but it needs to be set up carefully. The goal is not to hide the phone. The goal is to route the right calls the right way when the line is overloaded.

Use this setup checklist:
1. Decide whether to forward all calls, only busy calls, or only unanswered calls.
2. Confirm the code with your carrier or phone system.
3. Test from a real phone.
4. Listen to the caller experience end to end.
5. Turn it off and retest when the rush is over.

Common phone setup examples include *72 to forward all calls on many landlines and some carriers, *73 to turn it off, **21*number# on some GSM mobile carriers to forward all calls, **61*number# for unanswered calls, and **67*number# for busy calls. Verizon Wireless often uses *72, *73, and *71 for busy or no-answer forwarding. Business VoIP systems usually set forwarding in the web portal. Codes vary by carrier and plan, so always confirm with your carrier and test with a call.

If you use ROAL, each location gets its own phone line automatically once you claim the host, and you can forward your existing number to it. The restaurant keeps its own number, and forwarding can be turned off any time.

sections.h2: How do I know the checklist is working once the rush starts?
sections.body:
The best busy season checklist is short enough to use during service. You should be able to glance at it, fix a problem, and keep moving. If it is too long, it will get ignored the minute tickets start stacking up.

Use this final day-of checklist:
- Phones are on the right greeting and hours.
- Menu prices and sold-out items are current.
- Staff know who handles phone orders, pickup handoff, and complaints.
- Kitchen screen or ticket flow is ready.
- Call forwarding settings are tested.
- Someone is watching for repeated questions or missed details.

A simple scorecard helps. At the end of a rush, count three things: how many calls came in, how many orders were cleanly taken, and how many problems had to be corrected later. You do not need fancy software to learn from that. Just write the numbers on paper or in a notes app and compare them week to week.

If you want a simple place to start, [build a free test host](/try) from your website, Google Maps link, or restaurant name and city. ROAL lets you test-call it in the browser with no sign-up needed, so you can hear how it handles your menu before the rush hits.

takeaways: Update phone, hours, and menu details before the rush starts.
Decide who handles orders, pickup handoff, and tricky questions.
Use call forwarding only after testing it with a real call.
Keep sold-out items and pricing current so callers get clear answers.
Use a short day-of checklist that staff can follow during service.

faq.q: What is the most important part of a restaurant busy season checklist?
faq.a: The most important part is phone and order flow. If callers cannot get the right hours, menu answers, or pickup timing, the rush gets harder for the kitchen and the front counter. Start with the phone, then move to staffing and menu updates.

faq.q: Should I forward all calls during busy season?
faq.a: Not always. Some restaurants forward all calls during the rush, while others only forward unanswered or busy calls. The right choice depends on your team size and phone volume, so test the setup first and make sure callers still get a clear answer.

faq.q: How do I keep phone orders from slowing down the kitchen?
faq.a: Use a clear order format: name, phone number, items, modifiers, notes, and ready time. Send the clean ticket straight to the kitchen screen or the person building tickets. That reduces mistakes and keeps the line moving.
